title: Wildlife, Site Visibility, Access and Security Planning

content.overview: Outdoor site planning includes animal damage, unintended human access, visibility and emergency access. Controls should be lawful, proportionate and designed before losses occur rather than creating unsafe barriers around the crop.

vocabulary.definition: Physical or procedural method intended to prevent unwanted animal or human entry.
Food, water, waste or habitat feature that can draw wildlife or pests.
Route allowing safe entry/exit for people or responders during an incident.

sections.title: Identify the actual local threat
sections.body: Wildlife pressure varies by region. Tracks, browsing patterns, local extension information and prior site history are stronger than generic assumptions.

sections.title: Reduce attractants and protect vulnerable stages
sections.body: Waste, standing water and unsecured inputs can draw animals. Young transplants may require different protection from established plants.

sections.title: Security cannot block safety
sections.body: Fencing, gates, cameras or visibility controls must comply with applicable rules and preserve lawful emergency access. Cannabis security requirements vary by jurisdiction.

workedExamples: Deer browsing may justify plant exclusion, while burrowing damage requires a different site response.
A locked perimeter without an emergency-access plan can create a new safety problem.
commonMistakes: Using one deterrent for every animal.
Leaving crop waste near the production zone.
Assuming privacy/security rules are the same everywhere.
content.practicalApplication: Document wildlife evidence, access points, attractants, legal/security requirements and emergency routes, then select controls matched to the identified risk.
content.summary: Outdoor security and wildlife management should reduce specific risks while preserving legality, safety and access.
